tone_statements.quote: Green, Anderson, & Obeng (2013) argue that the word‑level RT patterns in Susu are most similar to those observed in Mende. That is, the last tone of W1 is copied onto the first TBU of W2. [...] A series of nearly identical outcomes is reported for Yalunka in Keita (1989). Thus, from the standpoint of word‑level RT, languages of the Soso‑Jalonke are well placed alongside most other Southwestern Mande languages. [para 113:] Bandi, Loko, Looma, Kpelle, Zialo, Susu, and Yalunka all behave in a manner that is reminiscent of Mende.

tone_statements.quote: Т о н. Практически все языки манде тональны (единственное известное исключение — один из говоров дьялонке на севере Фута-Джаллона, утративший тоны под влиянием пулар; описан Фредерике Люпке), однако инвентарь (от 2 до 5 уровневых тонов, в некоторых языках есть и контурные тоны) и функциональная нагрузка тонов очень сильно варьируют; [...] В большинстве языков западной ветви манде имеется два уровневых тона [...]. tone_statements.translation: Tone. Practically all Mande languages are tonal (the only known exception is one of the Jalonke (Dialonke) varieties in the north of Fouta Djallon, which lost its tones under the influence of Pular; described by Friederike Luepke), but the inventory (from 2 to 5 level tones, some languages also have contour tones) and the functional load of tone vary greatly; [...] Most languages of the Western branch of Mande have two level tones [...]. [p. 21:] Dialonke (Yalunka; self-designation jalonke, yalunka) [...] One of the northern varieties (which has lost tone) was described by Friederike Luepke, the north-eastern (Malian) dialect by Denis Creissels (dictionary) and Boniface Keita
tone_statements.locator: p. 34 (volume; overview chapter 'Манде языки', prosody paragraph 'Тон'), plus p. 21 (paragraph 'Дьялонке')

readall_conflicts: No source says anything about word stress, so there is no disagreement on stress. The sources do disagree on tone by variety: Lüpke 2005 (thesis, pp. 84-87) shows with pitch tracks and comprehension experiments that the Jalonke of Saare Kindia, Guinea, has no lexical or grammatical tone, while Creissels 1989 (p. 20), Creissels 2010 and Keita 1987/88, 1989 describe the Dialonké of Faléya, Mali, as a two-register tone language (H/B) with elaborate tone-realisation rules; Lüpke herself notes the difference and treats it as tone loss in the Guinean variety. The listed work (Lüpke 2005, LDD 3) is a corpus-methodology article and is silent on both stress and tone.

sources.citation: Keïta, Boniface. 1987/88. Morphologie de la forme définie des noms en dialonké. Mandenkan 14-15: 205-215.
sources.note: Morphology of the definite suffix -na with tonal realisation rules (H-tone spreading etc.). Nothing on stress or accent (scanned; image-only PDF).

sources.citation: Creissels, Denis. 2010. Liste lexicale du dialonké de Faléya. Mandenkan 46: 49-71.
sources.note: Tone-marked wordlist; intro (pp. 49-50) says Lüpke's variety 'diffère essentiellement du dialonké de Faléya par la perte des distinctions tonales notées dans ce lexique', and that only heavy syllable rhymes can bear BH/HB sequences. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Lüpke, Friederike. 2005. Small is beautiful: contributions of field-based corpora to different linguistic disciplines, illustrated by Jalonke. LDD 3: 75-105.
sources.note: Open-access article that reuses the tone experiments; could contain a prosodic characterisation (stress/intonation) absent from the thesis; blocked only by a bot wall.

sources.citation: Creissels, Denis. 1989. Structures syllabiques du dialonké de Faléya. Mandenkan 18: 1-30.
sources.note: Dialonké of Faléya (Kéniéba, Mali) is tonal: 'Le dialonké a un système tonal réductible à deux unités tonologiques de base, |H| et |B|' (p. 20, §7); CV syllables carry one tone, CV:/CVC syllables may carry HB or BH; tone-realisation rules (H-spreading, lowering) described pp. 20-28. No statement about stress/accent in Dialonké; 'accentuation' is mentioned only for Latin/Arabic as a comparison (p. 20).

sources.citation: Keita, Boniface. 1989. La compacité tonale en dialonké. Mandenkan 18: 205-215.
sources.note: Tonal compactness (tone of compound/genitive constructions) in Dialonké; floating tones, H/B schemes. Nothing on stress or accent (scanned, English model; image-only PDF).

sources.note: Second-hand summary (citing Luepke, Creissels, Keita): practically all Mande languages are tonal, the single known exception being one northern Jalonke variety on the Fouta Djallon that lost tone under Pular (Fula) influence (Luepke's); most Western Mande languages have two level tones; p. 21 repeats that Luepke's northern variety 'has lost tones' while the NE (Malian) dialect is described by Creissels and Keita (whose works, in the works listed here, mark two tones). Also states stress is absent in most Mande languages.
